narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) of your class, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA came next. At 3.00 it was modestly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, and this slightly lowered the predicted risk of failure. However, the positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your class rank.

Finally, your family income bracket of upper-middle class worked modestly in your favor compared with students from lower brackets, but its influence was smaller than the other two factors.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic performance trajectory made success on the bar exam uncertain. To strengthen future applications, focus on raising your class rank in the remaining years, improving your LSAT score well above 27, and consider part-time work if it allows more study time. These steps can meaningfully shift your profile before you reapply. (248 words)
